title: I finally built a backtest that made me feel like a genius. Took me a week to realize it was quietly lying to me in about 5 different ways.
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext:
So last month I coded up this mean reversion thing I'd been sitting on for a while. Nothing exotic. Ran it over a few years of data, hit go, and the equity curve that came back was honestly gorgeous. Smooth, barely any drawdown, Sharpe way higher than anything I'd made before. I sat there for a second feeling like I'd cracked it.  
And that feeling is exactly what saved me, because it was too good. If it was really that easy I would not be the guy discovering it on a Tuesday night. So instead of funding it I spent the next week trying to prove my own backtest wrong, and I found five separate ways it had been cheating. Writing them down in case it saves someone else the same gut punch.  
The first one I caught was look-ahead. I was making the entry decision on the daily bar using that day's close, which felt totally normal until I realized that in real life, at the moment I would actually be deciding, that candle hadn't closed yet. I was letting my strategy peek at information it would never have had. Fixing just that one thing knocked a chunk off the returns immediately.  
Then I looked at my universe and felt kind of stupid. I was testing on the stocks that exist today. Which means every company that went to zero or got delisted over my test window was just invisible. My list was secretly pre-filtered to only include survivors, so of course a strategy looked good on it. The dogs that would have blown up my account weren't even in the data.  
The one that actually stung was overfitting. I went back and counted how many little variations I'd tried before landing on the "winning" settings, and it was a lot. When you try that many combinations, one of them is going to look amazing by pure luck, and I'd fooled myself into thinking I'd found signal when I'd really just found the noise that happened to fit my particular slice of history. The tell was that if I nudged any parameter even slightly, the magic fell apart. Real edges don't shatter that easily.  
Fourth, I'd basically assumed trading was free, which is a fantasy, and it hit my strategy harder because it traded a lot. Once I put in a realistic spread and slippage guess, a bunch of the profit just evaporated. I'm doing a whole separate write-up on that one because it deserves it.  
And last, I finally did the honest test I'd been avoiding, which is checking it on data it had never touched during all my tinkering. Some of the edge held, a lot of it didn't. That out-of-sample chunk is the only number I actually trust now.  
The lesson I walked away with is that if a result only looks good under one exact set of knobs, it's noise in a costume. What checks do you all run before you let yourself believe a curve? I feel like I learned all five of these the hard way and I'd rather steal your process than keep faceplanting.

comments.author: greenmatrix86
comments.body:
The overfitting and cost ones hit close to home for us too. On overfitting — the check we lean on is whether a change holds up on a completely separate, untouched period, not just the one you tuned it on. We've had parameter changes that looked great on the data we optimized against and straight up flipped sign on a later, held-out chunk — if it only works with the exact knobs you landed on, it's not a real rule.

On costs — we found real execution costs eat a lot more than a generic spread guess suggests, especially for anything that leans heavily on getting stopped out rather than exiting cleanly at an observed price. Worth checking which of your exit types actually carry that risk instead of applying one blanket cost assumption to everything.
